claims.text: The untreated AlCoCrFeNi-type eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical dual-phase lamellar microstructure.
The untreated alloy experiences dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries.
Dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries cause local stress concentrations, microcracking, and brittle failure in the untreated alloy.
Adding approximately 0.5–1 at.% Zr and annealing near 600°C for about 30 minutes will form Zr-rich nanoprecipitates.
The resulting Zr-rich nanoprecipitates will be nanoscale, coherent, uniformly distributed, and located along interlamellar interfaces.
Real-time in situ adjustment of the annealing parameters can ensure formation of the desired nanoprecipitates.
Zr-rich nanoprecipitates will function as dislocation sinks or deflectors.
The nanoprecipitates will prevent excessive dislocation pile-ups at phase boundaries.
Reducing dislocation pile-ups will reduce localized stress concentrations and microcrack initiation.
Deflection of dislocations by the nanoprecipitates will promote cross-slip and more homogeneous plastic deformation.
The nanoprecipitates will provide precipitation hardening that preserves or increases yield strength.
Relative to the untreated alloy, the treated alloy will have significantly greater room-temperature tensile ductility.
Relative to the untreated alloy, the treated alloy will have similar or moderately improved yield and ultimate tensile strengths.
The treated alloy will exhibit delayed microcrack initiation and propagation.
The predicted improvements apply under quasi-static room-temperature tensile loading at approximately 10^-3 s^-1 and under moderate cyclic loading.
Inadequate control of precipitate size and distribution may produce coarsening or inhomogeneity and thereby degrade the outcome.
Related literature on high-entropy alloys and aluminum alloys supports precipitation hardening and dislocation-management mechanisms relevant to the hypothesis.
